title: Performance of predictive AI-based clinical decision support systems across clinical domains: A systematic review and meta-analysis
explain_beginner: Researchers combined results from 50 studies of AI tools that help doctors make predictions or decisions. These tools covered 17 medical areas. On average, the tools were fairly good at ruling conditions out when they said a condition was absent, but their overall ability to tell sick from not sick was modest. Their results varied widely between studies. Only about one quarter were tested in real clinical settings before deployment, and most reported technical scores rather than how care changed. This matters because strong lab results do not guarantee that these tools improve patient care in everyday practice.
explain_business: For executives, this review shows that evidence for predictive AI decision support improving clinical performance is still limited. Across 50 studies, the average ability to separate cases was modest, though the tools were better at confirming when a condition was absent. Most evidence came from retrospective work, and only about a quarter involved prospective deployment. Many studies did not report how workflows or patient outcomes changed. The practical decision is to treat headline accuracy claims cautiously, require prospective testing in your setting, ask for workflow and outcome evidence, and use structured evaluation before scaling. The proposed ROADMAP framework can guide evaluation, monitoring, and economic assessment.
explain_practitioner: The authors reviewed PubMed and Cochrane Library records through December 2024, screening 3,296 items and including 50 studies across 17 specialties. They assessed quality with QUADAS-2 and pooled performance using random effects. The combined AUC was 0.652, with specificity 0.819, accuracy 0.765, and sensitivity 0.660. Heterogeneity was very high for every measure, with I squared at or above 98.9 percent. Just under a quarter tested the tool prospectively in care, while nearly two thirds gave only technical scores and no workflow information. The authors propose the seven part ROADMAP framework to guide development, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, economics, and reporting.
